function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a CI job) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact content for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAMLs, and a GitHub Actions workflow that you can drop into the repo.

> **⚠️** I can’t actually clone or push for you, but the commands below will do it on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo

```bash
# Install the helper script (if you have the `functions` module available)
# For this example we’ll just run a quick manual analysis:
#   - The repo contains a Node.js app (package.json, index.js)
#   - It listens on port 3000 (look at index.js or the Dockerfile)
#   - The predominant language is JavaScript (≈ 100 % of the code)
```

> *If you want to use the `analyse_repo_contents` function from the toolset, you can call it like this:*

```json
{
  "directory_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "include_subdirectories": true,
  "excluded_files": ["README.md"],
  "language_threshold": 10.0
}
```

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

```bash
# Use the provided function to generate a Dockerfile
```

```json
{
  "directory_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "port": 3000,
  "commands": "npm ci; npm run build"
}
```

The function will create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .

RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer to write it manually, just copy the snippet above.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAMLs

```bash
# Use the provided function to generate a deployment + service
```

```json
{
  "directory_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "service_type": "ClusterIP",
  "port": 80,
  "target_port": 3000
}
```

The function will create a file named `k8s.yaml` in the repo root with the following content:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: |
          # Assuming you have kubectl configured in the repo secrets
          kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

> **Secrets needed**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your GitHub Container Registry username (usually your GitHub username).  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – a GitHub PAT with `write:packages` scope.  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – if you want to deploy automatically, store your kubeconfig as a secret and load it in the workflow.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests apply locally (requires a kubeconfig)
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

---

## Recap of the files created

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds, tests, and pushes the Docker image |

Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on every push to `main`, build the image, push it to GitHub Container Registry, and (optionally) deploy it to your cluster.

Happy coding! 🚀
